semantic_correction.stem: Two family members are brought to the emergency department after being found in an enclosed garage where a gasoline-powered generator was running. Both report headache, dizziness, and nausea; one is confused. A standard pulse oximeter reads 99%. Which action should the nurse take?

options.A: Administer high-flow 100% oxygen immediately and obtain blood co-oximetry while urgent evaluation continues.
options.B: Withhold oxygen because the pulse oximeter is normal and wait for a carboxyhemoglobin result before treating.
options.C: Apply low-flow oxygen only if the pulse oximeter falls below the usual hypoxemia range during observation.
options.D: Continue room-air observation and repeat pulse oximetry after rest because a normal reading makes serious exposure unlikely.

semantic_correction.rationale: Carbon monoxide poisoning should be suspected when multiple people from the same enclosed environment develop compatible neurologic and constitutional symptoms after a combustion exposure. Current NCBI Carbon Monoxide Poisoning guidance updated June 18, 2026 states that standard pulse oximetry cannot distinguish oxyhemoglobin from carboxyhemoglobin and may therefore produce falsely reassuring readings. Blood co-oximetry is used to measure carboxyhemoglobin, but treatment should not wait for confirmation when clinical suspicion is high. Initial management includes immediate removal from the source and prompt administration of high-flow 100% oxygen. Because these clients have a strong exposure history and compatible symptoms, a normal standard pulse-oximeter reading does not rule out toxicity. The nurse should begin 100% oxygen and obtain co-oximetry while urgent neurologic/cardiac evaluation continues rather than delay oxygen or use the standard SpO2 value as a treatment gate. The 2026 NCSBN NCLEX-RN Test Plan includes emergency-care procedures and management of impaired ventilation/oxygenation under Physiological Adaptation. Therefore A is the uniquely best response.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Suspect carbon monoxide poisoning from compatible symptoms and enclosed combustion exposure even when standard pulse oximetry is normal; begin high-flow 100% oxygen immediately and obtain blood co-oximetry without delaying treatment.

semantic_correction.source_locator: NCBI Carbon Monoxide Poisoning > Introduction/Evaluation/Initial Management — standard pulse oximetry cannot distinguish oxyhemoglobin from carboxyhemoglobin and may be falsely reassuring; confirm exposure with blood co-oximetry when possible; initiate high-flow 100% oxygen promptly. NCBI Carbon Monoxide Toxicity > Evaluation/Treatment and Management — bedside oxygen saturation cannot be relied upon; supplemental oxygen is the cornerstone and should begin without delay. NCSBN 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan > Physiological Adaptation, printed p. 46 / PDF p. 50 — perform emergency-care procedures and manage impaired ventilation/oxygenation.

audit_findings_append.finding: The replacement tests direct emergency recognition and treatment. Current NCBI guidance supports immediate 100% oxygen for suspected carbon monoxide poisoning and explicitly warns that standard pulse oximetry can be falsely reassuring.

scope_exclusions.carboxyhemoglobin_threshold: No COHb cutoff is used to decide whether to start oxygen; treatment begins from the strong exposure history and compatible symptoms while co-oximetry is obtained.
scope_exclusions.hyperbaric_oxygen: No hyperbaric-oxygen indication, pressure, treatment duration, pregnancy criterion, neurologic threshold, or COHb threshold is tested.
scope_exclusions.oxygen_device_details: The item requires high-flow 100% oxygen but does not prescribe a device flow rate, ventilation mode, or intubation threshold.
scope_exclusions.smoking_baseline: No smoker/non-smoker baseline COHb range is used because it is unnecessary for the immediate nursing action.

near_duplicate_check.note: Targeted GitHub search for 'carbon monoxide pulse oximetry normal 100% oxygen co-oximetry generator' returned no indexed repository match. Q0975 was considered because Q1350 replaces another informed-consent item; Q0975 tests informed-consent disclosure, whereas Q1350 tests carbon-monoxide emergency recognition and oxygen treatment. No broad bank rescan was performed.

option_audit.A: Correct. It treats suspected carbon monoxide toxicity immediately and obtains the appropriate blood measurement without relying on standard SpO2.
option_audit.B: Plausible confirmation-first approach, but oxygen treatment should not wait for the COHb result and a normal standard pulse-oximeter reading is not reassuring in CO poisoning.
option_audit.C: Plausible oxygen-titration approach for ordinary hypoxemia, but standard pulse oximetry is unreliable for detecting carboxyhemoglobinemia and should not gate treatment.
option_audit.D: Plausible observation strategy if exposure were unlikely, but the shared enclosed-combustion exposure plus symptoms create strong suspicion and the normal SpO2 does not exclude toxicity.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. B, C and D all rely on standard pulse oximetry or laboratory delay despite a strong exposure pattern. A alone begins source-supported treatment immediately while obtaining the correct diagnostic measurement.

cueing_check.note: Exact character counts were calculated from the stored strings. The correct option is not longest and all alternatives are parallel oxygen/evaluation decisions.
